Package Holiday Scam UK: Spot a Fake Travel Deal

Fraudsters are cashing in on holiday dreams with fake package deals — but there are reliable ways to check if your bargain is genuine.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-12 · Updated 2026-07-26 · 6 min read

Quick answer: A cheap package advertised by an unfamiliar seller and payable by bank transfer is high risk, but check more than the seller's name. An agent can sell under another company's ATOL. Verify the ATOL holder named on the certificate, then confirm the flight, hotel and operator independently. Contact your bank promptly if anything fails those checks.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a package holiday scam looks like

A package holiday scam advertises a flight, accommodation, and often extras bundled at a price far below any genuine travel company, then takes payment for a trip that does not exist or is never properly booked. An example of the style is: 7 nights all-inclusive in Turkey, flights included, £199pp — limited deals, pay by bank transfer to secure.

You may be given a convincing-looking but fake booking confirmation, only to discover no genuine booking exists. This guide shows the warning signs, how to book safely, and what to do if you have already paid.

Why these scams are convincing

An unusually low all-inclusive price is tempting, especially near school holidays, and a fake confirmation email or PDF itinerary can look identical to a genuine one. A seller who claims to have bulk operator rates or a special allocation sounds like they have access to a deal you cannot get elsewhere.

The fact that protects you: a qualifying package holiday that includes a flight and is sold by or through an ATOL holder should be ATOL protected, and you should receive an ATOL Certificate as soon as you pay anything, including a deposit. The certificate names the ATOL holder providing that protection, and you can check that holder independently before you part with more money.

Signs a package holiday deal is a scam

  • The price is far below any genuine travel company for the same holiday.
  • You are asked to pay by bank transfer to a personal account rather than through a recognised travel company.
  • The seller will not name the ATOL holder providing protection for a flight-inclusive package, or gives details that do not match the certificate.
  • You are pressured to book quickly because the deal is "about to expire".
  • The booking confirmation cannot be verified with the airline, hotel, or tour operator directly.
  • The company has no verifiable address, landline, or Companies House record.

How the scam works

First, an advert or message offers a bargain package holiday. Second, you pay, usually by bank transfer, to secure the deal. Third, you may receive a fake booking confirmation or itinerary. Fourth, when you try to check with the airline, hotel, or operator directly, no booking exists. Finally, the seller stops responding, sometimes just before the travel date.

Checking ATOL protection, the ATOL holder details, and the booking directly with the airline, hotel, or tour operator before you rely on it breaks the chain.

How to book a package holiday safely

Book through a recognised, ATOL-protected travel company.

  • Ask whether the flight-inclusive package is ATOL protected and who the ATOL holder is before you pay, then search that name or number in the official ATOL check.
  • Remember a travel agent may sell on behalf of another company's ATOL and does not need one of its own, so check the holder named on the certificate rather than only the shop front.
  • Make sure an ATOL Certificate actually arrives when you pay, and that the trip, passengers and holder on it match what you booked.
  • Book through a well-known travel agent or tour operator's own website, not a personal seller found on social media or a classified ad.
  • Verify any booking confirmation directly with the airline, hotel, or operator named in it.
  • Be suspicious of an all-inclusive price dramatically below every other source for the same trip.
  • Prefer paying by card, which offers more practical dispute options than a bank transfer.

If you are unsure, our Fake Airline Ticket Scam UK: Spot a Bargain Flight Con and Fake Travel Agent Scams UK: How to Spot Booking Fraud guides cover related travel-booking cons.

If you have already paid

Save the advert, messages, payment record and every itinerary or certificate before the listing disappears, then contact your bank. If ATOL protection was claimed, check the certificate for the name and number of the ATOL holder providing it. A travel agent may sell on behalf of another ATOL holder, so search both the seller and the disclosed holder and confirm the relationship with the holder using contact details you found independently. If no certificate was supplied, ask the agent why and seek advice from the CAA.

A package holiday is usually paid for weeks or months ahead of departure, so there is often more time to act than with a last-minute purchase. Then work through the payment, account and identity steps in the scam recovery checklist.

How to report a package holiday scam (UK)

Tell the platform that carried the advert, and tell the airline, hotel or tour operator named on the confirmation. Notifying the named supplier helps it investigate misuse of its brand.

If the seller quoted an ATOL number or claimed ATOL protection, report that to the CAA as well: it licenses ATOL holders and runs the search that would have shown whether the licence was real.

If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk, or on 0300 123 2040, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. The scam recovery checklist has the phishing email and text-forwarding routes and the steps that follow a report.

Frequently asked questions

Is it ever genuine to book a package holiday from someone on social media?

Treat it as high risk. Book through a recognised, ATOL-protected travel company or tour operator's own website instead. A stranger offering a bargain package holiday on social media is a common scam pattern.

Does ATOL protect every package holiday?

No. ATOL is for qualifying flight-inclusive package trips sold by or through an ATOL holder, and you should receive an ATOL Certificate. Non-flight packages and ordinary travel disputes are different. A travel agent can sell a protected trip on another company's ATOL, so ask who the ATOL holder is and check that holder before paying.

I have a booking confirmation — does that mean the holiday is real?

No. Contact the airline, hotel or tour operator through details you found independently and ask it to confirm what has actually been booked. For an ATOL-protected trip, you should also receive an ATOL Certificate as soon as you pay. A missing or inconsistent certificate is a serious warning; check the named ATOL holder and ask the CAA for advice rather than assuming the document or its absence settles the question by itself.

I've already paid for a package holiday that turned out to be fake — can I get my money back?

Sometimes. If a credit agreement funded the holiday, Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may apply: it needs the required relationship between the credit and the supplier, and a cash price of more than £100 and no more than £30,000, counted per item or qualifying set. Paying on credit does not guarantee cover, because intermediaries and the exact debtor-creditor-supplier relationship can affect a claim. Otherwise ask your card issuer about chargeback, which is a card-scheme process with scheme-set deadlines rather than a legal right. Where an eligible domestic consumer payment left by Faster Payments or CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024, the mandatory APP reimbursement rules may apply, subject to their exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a 13-month outer reporting limit and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Report it as soon as you can and keep the advert, the confirmation and the payment receipt.

How do I report a fake package holiday deal?

Start with the platform that hosted the advert, then tell the airline, hotel or operator named on the confirmation so it can investigate misuse of its brand. If an ATOL number or ATOL protection was claimed, tell the CAA. A financial loss goes to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

Fast checks

  • Pause before sending money or credentials
  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
